macroSectors.description: Covers the businesses that keep people healthy in India: making medicines and medical devices, running hospitals and diagnostic labs, and doing research work for the global drug industry. Demand is less tied to the economic cycle than most sectors, though exports and regulation make some parts volatile.

Covers companies that build, run, sell and support software, technology-enabled services and computing hardware. Much of its revenue comes from overseas clients, so global corporate technology budgets and the rupee shape results.

sectors.description: Groups pharmaceuticals and biotechnology, medical equipment and supplies, and healthcare services such as hospitals, diagnostics and contract research. Earnings come from domestic patients as well as large export markets, and regulators in India and abroad decide who can sell what.

Groups IT software (services and consulting, and software products), IT-enabled services such as engineering R&D and hosting, and IT hardware makers and distributors. Services firms are asset-light and people-driven, while hardware businesses carry heavy inventory and working capital.

industries.description: Makers of medicines and biological products, from chemical generics and APIs to biologics, vaccines and enzymes.
industries.businessOverview: Indian drug makers are large global suppliers of affordable generic medicines and active ingredients. At home they build prescription brands through doctor-facing sales teams; abroad they win approvals to supply generics to regulated and emerging markets. Biotechnology firms use living systems to make biologics, biosimilars, vaccines and enzymes, which need longer development and costlier plants. Quality compliance and regulatory approvals sit at the centre of the business model.

industries.description: Makers of medical devices, implants, disposables and lab consumables used by hospitals, labs and clinics.
industries.businessOverview: Companies range from high-volume disposables such as syringes and catheters to implants, dental products, lab plasticware and diagnostic equipment. Consumables bring repeat revenue, while equipment sales depend on hospital spending plans. India still imports much of its advanced equipment, and government policy aims to build local manufacturing. Exports of quality-certified, low-cost disposables are an important outlet.
keyRisks: Competition from imports and global brands

industries.description: Providers of care and health-related services: hospitals, diagnostic and other care providers, and research and analytics firms serving the drug industry.
industries.businessOverview: Hospitals and diagnostic chains serve patients directly and earn treatment and test fees paid by patients, insurers and government schemes. Their economics depend on how fully they use costly beds, machines and skilled staff. The industry also includes contract research, testing and analytics providers that sell services to pharma and biotech companies worldwide. Brand trust, doctor relationships and quality accreditation matter across the group.

industries.description: Companies that provide software services and consulting, or sell their own software products.
industries.businessOverview: Most listed firms are IT services exporters that build and maintain technology systems for global businesses using India-based engineering teams, billed in foreign currency through long contracts and projects. A smaller group owns software products sold as licences or subscriptions, which earn higher margins once a product scales. Talent, client relationships and keeping pace with shifts such as cloud and AI decide success.

industries.description: Companies delivering technology-enabled services such as engineering R&D, data hosting and digital process work.
industries.businessOverview: IT-enabled services firms combine skilled staff with IT infrastructure to do work for clients: designing products for manufacturers, hosting data and applications, or handling digital and back-office tasks. Engineering work is largely exported, while hosting and data-centre businesses mostly serve Indian enterprises and government. People-based models are asset-light; infrastructure-based models need heavy capital. Dependence on a few large clients is common.

industries.description: Makers, assemblers and distributors of computers, servers, printers and related equipment.
industries.businessOverview: The industry largely imports components or finished devices, then assembles or distributes them and supports customers with service. Distributors run high-volume, thin-margin businesses where inventory and credit control decide profits. Government incentives and procurement preferences encourage local manufacturing. Demand depends on replacement cycles, enterprise and government budgets and the spread of digitisation.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make medicines: the active ingredient (API or bulk drug) or finished tablets, capsules and injections. Most Indian firms make generics, copies of off-patent drugs.
productsAndServices: Generics for regulated and emerging markets
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream to downstream: turns chemical intermediates (often imported) into APIs and finished doses for distributors, chemists, hospitals and overseas buyers.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: At home they build doctor-prescribed brands via medical representatives; abroad they win approvals and supply low-cost generics, earning more on first-to-market or hard-to-make products.
revenueSources: API sales to other drug makers
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Patients via doctors, chemists and hospitals in India; wholesalers, pharmacy chains and tenders abroad; other drug makers for APIs.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Medicine use is steady and rises with ageing, chronic disease and insurance; in exports, the number of approved rivals per molecule sets how fast prices fall.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Strongly export-linked, so the rupee and US pricing matter; many raw materials are imported, notably from China.
basicIndustries.capexNote: GMP-grade plants and R&D labs need steady spending, though less than heavy industry.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Large inventories across many products and long supply chains, plus receivables from overseas distributors and stockists.
basicIndustries.regulation: CDSCO and state drug controllers license plants and products; NPPA caps essential-medicine prices under the DPCO; exports need USFDA, EU or WHO-GMP approval.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Strong doctor-facing brands, a clean regulatory record, low-cost integrated plants and complex products are hard to copy.

drivers.impact: US price erosion or shortages swing export margins.
USFDA inspections decide whether plants can ship to regulated markets.
A weaker rupee lifts export value but raises imported input costs.
Wider access to doctors and insurance lifts domestic prescriptions.
Price controls cap essential-drug prices; PLI aids local APIs.

risks.detail: A warning letter or import alert can halt a plant's exports.
More rivals on a molecule push prices down fast.
Concentrated sourcing of starting materials exposes cost and supply.
Litigation brings legal costs or delayed launches.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Medicine demand holds up in downturns, though export pricing and regulatory events make profits lumpy.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that use living cells, microbes or enzymes to make biologic medicines, biosimilars, vaccines, enzymes and probiotics. It is science-heavy and slower to scale than chemical drug making.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream: buys cell lines, culture media, reagents and bioprocess equipment, and supplies drug makers, food and feed processors, hospitals and governments.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They sell hard-to-make biological products at premium prices, or charge global clients to develop and make biologics; a few products often drive most profit.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Pharma partners, hospitals and governments for biologics and vaccines; food, feed, textile and detergent makers for enzymes.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand grows as big biologics lose patents and industries swap chemical processes for enzymes; scarce talent, long plant qualification and slow approvals limit supply.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Tied to regulated export markets and global partners; key inputs and equipment are mostly imported, so the rupee matters.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Bioreactors, cleanrooms and long validation make plants costly and slow to bring online.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Development absorbs cash long before revenue; biologics need cold-chain storage and partner milestones are lumpy.
basicIndustries.regulation: CDSCO approves biologics and vaccines; genetically engineered organisms and products need clearance from RCGM and GEAC; export products need USFDA or European approval and inspections.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Proprietary strains or cell lines, process know-how, approved plants and a regulatory record take years to build.

drivers.impact: Big biologics going off-patent open markets for biosimilars.
Approval timelines and inspections decide when products start earning.
Overseas biotech funding drives contract development demand.
Cell, gene and mRNA therapies can raise or reduce the value of existing platforms.

risks.detail: A product can fail in trials after years of spending.
Slow or rejected approvals push revenue out.
Prices fall as more makers launch the same molecule.
Failed biological batches are costly.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: End demand is steady, but funding cycles, partner decisions and approvals make earnings uneven.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make the physical tools of healthcare, from syringes, catheters and gloves to implants, dental products, diagnostic machines and lab plasticware.
productsAndServices: Syringes, cannulas, catheters and other disposables
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream: converts medical-grade plastics, steel, electronics and chemicals into devices, and sells to hospitals, labs, clinics, distributors and overseas device brands.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Most earn repeat revenue from consumables used on every patient; equipment makers add machine sales, servicing and the consumables machines need.
revenueSources: Exports to distributors and device brands
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Hospitals, clinics, diagnostic labs, dentists, research labs and public health programmes in India and overseas.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Volumes rise with hospital beds, surgeries, testing and infection-control norms; local makers compete with imported global brands on cost and service.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Many firms export disposables to regulated markets, while advanced equipment and electronic parts are largely imported.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Cleanroom moulding, sterilisation and automated lines need investment, though less than drug or biotech plants.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Many products and sizes push up inventory, and payments from hospitals and government tenders can be slow.
basicIndustries.regulation: CDSCO licenses devices by risk class under the Medical Devices Rules; NPPA caps some prices such as stents and knee implants; exports need CE or USFDA clearance; PLI aids local makers.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Regulatory approvals, doctor familiarity with a product, wide distribution and low-cost precision manufacturing protect established firms.

drivers.impact: More hospitals, surgeries and tests raise device and consumable use.
PLI, local-preference procurement and import duties favour domestic makers.
Global buyers diversifying suppliers support disposable exports.
Polymer and metal costs move margins on low-priced disposables.

risks.detail: Government price controls can cut realisations.
Global brands win on technology, cheap imports on price.
Quality failures trigger recalls and lost hospital trust.
Government tenders bring price pressure and payment delays.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Daily-use consumables are defensive, while equipment purchases follow hospital budgets and expansion plans.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that run hospitals: multi-speciality chains and single-speciality centres such as eye, heart, cancer, fertility or mother-and-child hospitals, treating admitted patients and outpatients.
productsAndServices: Speciality care such as cardiac, cancer, eye and IVF
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Downstream: buys medicines, devices, consumables and doctors' time, and serves patients directly; bills are paid by patients, insurers and government schemes.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They fill beds with complex, higher-paying treatments; profit depends on occupancy, revenue per occupied bed and staff costs, and mature hospitals earn far more than new ones.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Self-paying patients, health insurers and TPAs, government schemes such as PM-JAY and CGHS, corporates and foreign patients.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand grows with chronic disease, ageing, insurance and preference for private care; scarce doctors, nurses and quality beds, plus long build times, limit supply.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Mostly domestic; medical tourism adds foreign revenue, and imported equipment ties some costs to the rupee.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Land, buildings and medical equipment are expensive, and new beds take years to fill.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Cash patients pay quickly, but insurers and government schemes pay with a delay; drug and consumable inventory is modest.
basicIndustries.regulation: State clinical-establishment, fire and pollution approvals; NABH accreditation; package rates fixed by PM-JAY and CGHS; IRDAI rules on cashless claims; NPPA price caps on some implants.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Reputation, well-known doctors, prime locations, accreditation and the years needed to build trust make established brands hard to challenge locally.

drivers.impact: Rising private health spending lifts footfall and complex procedures.
More insured patients can afford costlier treatment.
Scheme rates and implant price caps affect revenue per patient.
Visa ease and flight links drive medical tourism.
Higher occupancy spreads fixed costs.

risks.detail: Losing key doctors can take patients away.
Caps on rates, implants or drugs cut revenue per patient.
New hospitals lose money until occupancy builds.
Negligence claims or billing disputes damage trust.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Most treatment cannot be postponed, though elective procedures and medical tourism can dip in bad times.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Healthcare businesses other than full hospitals: mainly diagnostic labs that test samples and centres that do scans, plus dialysis and home-care providers and some test-kit makers.
productsAndServices: Radiology: X-ray, ultrasound, CT and MRI
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Downstream: buys analysers, reagents and scanners from equipment makers and sells test results and care to patients, doctors, hospitals and public programmes.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They charge per test or session; collection centres feed central labs (hub-and-spoke), so profit rises as more tests run through the same machines and staff.
revenueSources: Testing for hospitals and smaller labs
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Individual patients, referring doctors, hospitals and smaller labs, employers, insurers and state health programmes.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand grows with chronic-disease monitoring, preventive-health awareness and insurance. The market is crowded with small standalone labs, and online test aggregators sharpen price competition.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Almost entirely domestic; analysers, reagents and imaging machines are often imported, so some costs move with the rupee.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Imaging machines and central labs need capital, but collection centres are light and often franchised.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Retail patients pay upfront; hospital and government contracts create receivables; reagent stocks are modest.
basicIndustries.regulation: NABL and NABH accreditation signal quality; ultrasound centres follow the PCPNDT Act; X-ray and CT units need AERB licences; biomedical-waste rules apply.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: A brand doctors trust, a dense collection network, accreditation and high volumes per lab give lower costs than small rivals.

drivers.impact: More testing and chronic-disease care raises volumes.
Regular check-ups bring repeat customers.
Aggregators and new entrants push down routine test prices.
Lab automation cuts costs; home testing changes how customers are reached.

risks.detail: Discounting by aggregators and new labs squeezes margins.
Wrong results damage the brand and can draw penalties.
New cities lose money until volumes build.
Volumes drop after temporary spikes such as epidemics.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Most tests are medically needed, though wellness and discretionary tests slow in weaker times.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that do research, testing and technology work for drug and biotech makers rather than selling medicines: contract research (CRO), contract manufacturing (CDMO), testing labs and pharma data services.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Upstream service partner to the drug industry: supplies scientists, labs and data to drug developers, and buys reagents, lab instruments and software.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They charge per project, per dedicated scientist (FTE model) or per milestone, and earn supply revenue when a client's molecule reaches the market.
revenueSources: Analytics and digital services to pharma
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Global pharma and biotech companies, Indian drug makers, food and consumer firms needing tests, and clinical-trial sponsors.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand depends on global R&D budgets, biotech funding and big pharma's push to outsource and diversify suppliers; supply depends on scientists and audit-ready labs.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Mainly exports services to US, European and Japanese clients, so the rupee, global R&D spending and supplier-diversification policies matter.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Lab- and plant-based research firms invest heavily, while analytics and technology service firms are asset-light.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Mostly client receivables and unbilled work; milestone billing makes cash flows lumpy.
basicIndustries.regulation: Trials follow CDSCO's clinical-trial rules; labs follow GLP and GMP norms and face client and USFDA audits; data work must meet privacy and pharmacovigilance requirements.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Long client relationships, a clean audit record, scientific depth and trusted data confidentiality make clients slow to switch.

drivers.impact: Bigger research budgets and more outsourcing lift project demand.
Booms and busts in overseas biotech funding move discovery orders.
Clients diversifying from China can shift work to India.
AI and data tools change drug discovery and pharma marketing.

risks.detail: Losing a large client or molecule hits revenue.
Failed trials or budget cuts end contracts early.
Competition for scientists pushes up wages.
A failed regulator or client audit can halt work.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Outsourcing is a long-term trend, but global biotech funding and pharma budgets move in cycles.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: IT services companies that build, run and maintain software and technology systems for businesses, mostly large overseas clients, using teams of engineers in India and abroad.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream services layer: works on global software and cloud platforms to deliver solutions for banks, insurers, retailers, manufacturers, telecom firms and governments.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They bill for people-time (time-and-material), fixed-price projects or multi-year managed-services deals. Margins depend on billing rates, staff utilisation and how much work is done offshore.
revenueSources: Resale of software licences and platforms
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Large and mid-sized firms in the US, Europe and elsewhere, mainly banking, insurance, retail, manufacturing, healthcare and telecom, plus Indian enterprises and government.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand follows global corporate technology budgets: run-the-business spending is sticky, discretionary projects get cut when client economies slow. Supply depends on hiring engineers.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Highly export-oriented: revenue mostly in dollars, euros and pounds, costs mostly in rupees, so currency moves flow into margins.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Spending goes mainly on offices, laptops and some data centres; people are the main asset.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Mostly client receivables and unbilled revenue; there is no physical inventory.
basicIndustries.regulation: Light in India (SEZ and STPI rules, labour laws, DPDP Act); overseas, work-visa rules such as H-1B and privacy laws such as GDPR affect delivery.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Deep client relationships, industry know-how, delivery scale and high vendor-switching costs protect leading firms.

drivers.impact: US and European client budgets set the pace of new deals.
A weaker rupee lifts revenue against India-based costs.
Cloud and AI create new work but shrink effort on older services.
Attrition and salary hikes move margins.

risks.detail: Slowdowns in key client industries delay projects and squeeze pricing.
Automation can shrink billable hours.
High staff turnover raises hiring and training costs.
Visa curbs or local-hiring rules raise delivery costs.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Long maintenance contracts give stability, but new projects follow the global business cycle.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that own and sell their own software, such as banking, lending or compliance platforms, business messaging platforms, digital maps and business apps, instead of renting out engineers.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Upstream in software: builds intellectual property and sells licences or subscriptions to banks, enterprises, telecom operators and governments, directly or through partners.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They earn licence fees, subscriptions, usage charges and annual maintenance; once built, each extra customer costs little to serve, so margins can widen with scale.
operatingCosts: Telecom carrier charges for messaging platforms
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Banks, NBFCs, insurers, enterprises, telecom operators, government bodies and small businesses in India and overseas.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand grows with digitisation of banking, payments and compliance and with the shift to cloud. Competition from global software vendors and open-source tools limits pricing.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: A mix of domestic and export customers; overseas sales earn foreign currency, and competition is global even at home.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Most investment is product development spending rather than plants or machinery.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Subscriptions help cash flow, but licence and implementation deals with banks and government can leave long receivables.
basicIndustries.regulation: Mostly light, but client-sector rules matter: RBI, SEBI and IRDAI norms shape financial software, TRAI rules govern commercial messaging, and the DPDP Act covers personal data.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Products embedded in client workflows, high switching costs, proprietary data and regulatory know-how protect leading firms.

drivers.impact: Cloud, AI and new platforms can open markets or make products obsolete.
Expanding lenders need more banking and lending software.
New compliance and reporting rules create regtech demand.
More online transactions and business messages raise usage revenue.

risks.detail: A better rival product can erode the customer base.
Large licence wins are irregular, so quarters can be uneven.
Bigger global vendors chase the same clients.
Reliance on telecom carriers or cloud providers can squeeze margins.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Recurring subscriptions are steady, but new licence sales slow when clients cut budgets.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that deliver services using IT systems and skilled staff, such as engineering R&D services, data-centre and cloud hosting, managed IT operations and digital back-office work.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream services: uses IT infrastructure and trained staff to support manufacturers, automotive and aerospace firms, enterprises and government; buys servers, power and connectivity.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They bill per engineer-hour, per project, per transaction or for hosting capacity used. Profit comes from keeping people or infrastructure well utilised.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Automotive, aerospace, industrial and technology companies for engineering work; enterprises, banks and government departments for hosting and processing.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand rises as companies outsource product engineering and move workloads to cloud and local data centres; supply depends on engineers and data-centre power.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Engineering services are largely exported and billed in foreign currency; hosting demand is mainly domestic, helped by data-localisation needs.
basicIndustries.capexNote: People-based services are asset-light, but data-centre and cloud operators are capital-heavy exceptions.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Mainly client receivables; government contracts can pay slowly.
basicIndustries.regulation: Light general regulation plus the DPDP Act; hosting for government and financial clients follows MeitY cloud empanelment and RBI data-localisation norms.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Deep know-how in specific client industries, long relationships, certified facilities and reliable delivery create switching costs.

drivers.impact: Global auto, aerospace and industrial R&D budgets drive engineering orders.
Electric vehicles, software-defined products and AI add engineering and data work.
Data localisation and digital government create local hosting demand.
Reliable, affordable power shapes data-centre expansion.
Export billing gains when the rupee weakens.

risks.detail: Many firms depend on a few large clients.
Downturns in auto or aerospace cut engineering budgets.
AI tools reduce the need for manual processing and content work.
Data-centre expansion needs heavy capital and power.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Hosting and managed services recur steadily, while engineering projects follow client investment cycles.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make, assemble or distribute computers and related equipment, such as PCs, laptops, servers, storage, printers, networking and satellite-communication gear, and industrial coding and marking printers.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream to downstream: imports chips, parts or finished devices from global brands, assembles or distributes them, and sells to resellers, integrators, enterprises and government.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Distributors earn thin margins on high volumes plus vendor incentives and credit services. Manufacturers earn on equipment sales, consumables and service contracts.
revenueSources: Consumables such as ink and ribbons
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Households and small businesses via resellers, enterprises, data centres, banks, government and schools, and factories using coding printers.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand follows PC refresh cycles, enterprise and government IT budgets and digitisation. Supply depends on global chip and component availability.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Heavily import-dependent for chips and components, so global component prices and the rupee matter; PLI encourages local assembly, including for export.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Assembly and distribution need modest fixed assets; the main capital need is working capital.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Heavy: large inventory, channel credit and slow government payments make working-capital control central.
basicIndustries.regulation: BIS compulsory registration for many electronics, the PLI scheme for IT hardware, import-authorisation rules for laptops and PCs, local-preference public procurement, and e-waste rules.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Distribution reach, vendor tie-ups, disciplined credit control, service networks and local manufacturing scale protect established players.

drivers.impact: New operating systems and AI-ready PCs drive replacements.
PLI, import rules and local-preference buying favour local assembly.
A weaker rupee raises import costs that may not pass through quickly.
Chip shortages limit supply and raise prices.
Household and small-business buying follows incomes and festive seasons.

risks.detail: Small price moves or stock losses can wipe out profit.
Fast product cycles force discounting of old stock.
Slow-paying partners or government buyers tie up cash.
Losing a key brand's distribution rights cuts revenue.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Buyers can postpone computer and equipment purchases when budgets tighten.
